2.add: A direct return after a winding 354.5 m outward path reflects a vector that sums every segment of the trip into one direction and one distance.

3.add: The test distinguishes movement-derived navigation from immediate attraction to the true nest, because the course expressed after release points where the nest would lie had the ant not been moved.

5.add: Because the error is systematic and not random scatter, the integrator follows a consistent rule that can be described mathematically.

third_paragraph.6: The error pattern persisted across compass conditions, which places the bias in the path-integration computation and not in one defective sky cue. Sun and polarized skylight are related but separable heading inputs to the same integrator.

7.add: A successful prediction for a new route geometry supports the approximate updating rule as a description of how the ant combines successive legs.

8.add: The ecological interpretation is that the approximation keeps homing errors small for the turning patterns an ant meets on a real foraging trip, and landmarks and searching cover the cases a home vector cannot.

9.add: Lengthened or shortened legs change the distance covered per stride on the inbound journey, which makes stride length the variable under test for the odometer.

11.add: The ant reads out the stored distance in the same stride units in which it acquired it.

12.add: All groups shared the same navigational task, so differences in homing distance can be assigned to the degree of leg shortening.

13.add: Shortened legs reduce how far each step advances the ant while the alternating pattern of the two supporting sets stays the same.

14.add: Stumps II removed more of the leg than stumps I and gave the shorter search, so greater shortening produced greater undershoot.

third_paragraph.15: Longer strides spread the search over more distance and shorter strides over less, so the width of the distribution scales with stride length as the centre does. Centre and width are two behavioral readouts of the same stride-based process.
third_paragraph.16: The dependence on journey history excludes a persistent injury as the explanation, because the same modified limbs gave accurate homing once outbound and inbound conditions matched. Stride-associated signals gathered on the way out are read out in the same units on the way back.

17.add: Expressing stride length relative to alitrunk length makes a stride comparable between large and small workers, so differences reflect the leg manipulation.

18.add: Longer strides at a given frequency carry the ant farther per cycle, so stride length is the quantity that the odometer must track.

20.add: The distance an ant covers depends on the strides actually taken, which vary with speed and with leg condition.

third_paragraph.21: Proprioceptive signals, limb-position feedback and the motor commands that generate the walking rhythm are the candidate inputs to the integrator. Each carries information proportional to stride, which is why a stride integrator can account for graded distance errors.
third_paragraph.22: The polarization filter over the learning-walk area controls one component of the compass environment while the ants behave naturally near the nest. Brains analysed after three days reflect the skylight experience each novice received.

23.add: Each schedule changes the polarization direction at a known rate, from a single 90° turn to continuous rotation at 15° per hour, so experience of change in the compass reference is the manipulated variable.

24.add: Anti-synapsin labels presynaptic sites and phalloidin labels actin, so microglomeruli and giant synapses appear as countable structures in defined neuropils.

third_paragraph.25: Counts of microglomeruli and giant synapses in defined neuropils reveal experience-associated reorganization of synaptic structure. Synapsin marks presynaptic boutons and actin marks target processes, so the two labels together define each synaptic complex.

26.add: The lateral-complex synaptic count responds to ultraviolet-containing light alone, whereas the central complex needs more than passive light, so the pathways differ in the experience that drives them.

third_paragraph.27: The central complex grows with the active experience of learning walks under natural skylight, a different requirement from the light exposure that suffices for lateral-complex giant synapses.

28.add: Any schedule in which polarization direction changes, whether one daily turn, hourly turns or continuous rotation, supports collar growth, so the mushroom body responds to change in the celestial compass reference.

third_paragraph.29: The lateral complex lies on the sky-compass pathway, and its giant synapses did not respond to rotation schedules that altered central-complex and collar measures. Experience shapes the higher centres differently from this earlier stage.
third_paragraph.30: The different transmitter identities of the lateral-complex projection and the mushroom-body input pathway are a proposed explanation for their different plasticity patterns, and the receptor type at each synapse sets the postsynaptic effect.

31.add: Comparing several magnetic conditions with dark interior-worker controls assesses experience-associated brain changes caused by the magnetic reference.

32.add: A downward vertical field alone does not supply a horizontal reference direction, so nest-directed pauses depend on the horizontal component.

33.add: Nest-directed gazes were lost with a vertical field alone and preserved with no field at all, so a partial magnetic cue and a complete absence of magnetic information have different effects on orientation.

third_paragraph.34: A magnetic vector that follows the solar azimuth still serves as a usable reference within each short learning walk, so nest-directed look-backs persist. The manipulation makes magnetic and celestial directions covary over the day, removing their natural changing angular relationship.

35.add: Central-complex growth required the natural changing relation between magnetic and celestial cues, which the sun-following vector removed, even though the ants could still look back toward the nest.

36.add: Collar growth in the natural field and its absence under altered magnetic conditions indicate that the directional reference available during learning walks influences how visual input circuitry develops.

third_paragraph.37: Natural magnetic direction and a fixed panorama stay constant while the sun and polarization pattern move, so they can serve as the fixed standard against which the moving sky compass is calibrated. The antennal Johnston’s organ is a candidate contributor to magnetoreception in this scheme.

40.add: A later directional shift cannot be attributed simply to entering that channel, because ants with one feeder search equally on both sides of it.

41.add: The early bias toward the side of the second feeder is what an ant using an alternative learned goal would show.

42.add: Ants widen their search toward a second stored goal when the first goal is absent, so each feeder is stored as its own destination.

43.add: Subtracting the one-feeder baseline isolates the part of the search attributable to the second feeder.

third_paragraph.44: The ongoing path integrator supplies the current nest-relative state and the stored vector supplies the target, so comparing them yields a heading toward B without a metric cognitive map.

45.add: The observed behavior is compatible with a nest-referenced vector system and does not require the stronger explanation of a metric cognitive map.

inserts.title: A home vector is a direction and a distance
paragraphs: A home vector is the direction and distance from the animal's current position back to its nest, computed continually from information gathered during movement. It is a single summary of the whole outward journey and does not store the sequence of turns that produced it.

Müller and Wehner recorded a natural foraging trip of _Cataglyphis fortis_ in Tunisia. The outward path measured 354.5 m and the maximum distance from the nest was 113.2 m. After finding food, the ant returned along a comparatively direct inbound route.

A direct return after a long winding outward path indicates that the ant did not retrace its steps. The difference between outward path length and nest displacement separates route retracing from vector-guided homing, and the ant updates the vector with every segment of the trip.
notes: The home vector is the quantity that path integration maintains.
Definition.
A home vector gives the direction and distance back to the nest.
Movement keeps updating it during the whole journey.
Not a memory of turns.
The vector summarizes the outward journey in one direction and one distance.
It does not store the order of the turns that produced it.
The recorded trip.
The ant was Cataglyphis fortis, tracked in Tunisia.
The outward path measured 354.5 meters.
Displacement from the nest.
The maximum distance from the nest was 113.2 meters.
The path was therefore much longer than the straight distance away.
The return.
After finding food the ant returned along a comparatively direct route.
It did not repeat the winding outward path.
Meaning.
Direct homing after a winding trip separates route retracing from vector-guided homing.
Why it matters for navigation.
An animal that stores only a vector needs very little memory for a long trip.
The vector can be used from any point on the outward path.

inserts.title: Systematic error differs from random scatter
paragraphs: Systematic error is a directional deviation that changes predictably with an experimental manipulation, such as the turning angle of the outward path. Random scatter varies unpredictably among journeys and has no relation to the manipulation. The two kinds of deviation call for different explanations.

Müller and Wehner trained ants on a 10 m leg followed by a 5 m leg and measured the angular difference between the true homeward direction and the expressed course. The error increased as the turning angle approached approximately 150° and reached about 20°.

The error returned toward zero at the limiting straight or reversed arrangements. A deviation that depends on turning angle in this orderly way indicates that the integrator follows a consistent rule that approximates the true homeward direction.
notes: Errors that follow a pattern reveal the rule the animal uses.
Definition.
Systematic error varies predictably with the manipulation.
Random scatter varies from journey to journey with no relation to it.
The measure.
The angular difference between the true homeward direction and the expressed course was recorded.
Ants had been trained through two-leg channels.
The route.
The first leg was 10 meters and the second was 5 meters.
The turning angle between legs was varied.
The pattern.
The error grew as the turning angle approached about 150 degrees.
It reached about 20 degrees in the published measurements.
The limits.
The error returned toward zero for the straight and the reversed arrangements.
Meaning.
An orderly relation between error and angle points to a consistent approximate updating rule.
Why the distinction matters.
Random scatter would be averaged away across many journeys.
Systematic error remains in the average and reveals the rule the integrator uses.
The training legs were channels, and release occurred in an open test field.
Summary.
Orderly error is evidence of a rule, and the rule is approximate.

inserts.title: Polarized skylight gives a compass direction
paragraphs: Polarized skylight is sky light whose electric field oscillates in a preferred orientation, and the pattern of orientations across the sky depends on the position of the sun. An ant can read a heading from this pattern even when direct sunlight is screened.

Müller and Wehner compared homing errors while ants used the sun, polarized skylight, or both. Screening the sun removed direct solar information, and painting the dorsal rim of the compound eyes removed access to the specialized polarization-sensitive eye region.

The 10 m and 5 m route still produced systematic errors in every condition. The bias in homing direction therefore arises in the path-integration process and does not depend on a single sky cue. Direct sunlight and polarization are related but separable compass inputs.
notes: The sky provides more than one directional signal.
Definition.
Polarization is the orientation of the electric field oscillation in a light wave.
Skylight has a pattern of such orientations across the sky.
Two cues.
Direct sunlight and the polarization pattern give related heading information.
They can be separated experimentally.
Removing the sun.
Screening the sun removed direct solar information.
Removing polarization.
Painting the dorsal rim of the compound eyes removed the specialized polarization-sensitive region.
Result.
The 10 meter and 5 meter route produced systematic errors in each condition.
Meaning.
The bias lies in the path-integration process and not in a single defective sky cue.
Why compare conditions.
Each condition removes a different part of the sky compass.
If one cue caused the bias, removing it would change the error pattern.
The pattern stayed, which points to the integrator itself.
Dorsal rim.
The dorsal rim of the compound eye is the specialized polarization-sensitive region.
Painting it removes access to polarized skylight.
Summary.
Related but separable cues feed one integrator.

inserts.title: An odometer estimates distance walked
paragraphs: An odometer is a mechanism for estimating distance traveled. In an ant it must convert locomotion into a distance, and one possible basis is the length and number of strides. A stride is one complete movement cycle of a particular leg.

Wittlinger and colleagues trained _Cataglyphis fortis_ to a feeder 10 m from the nest. At the feeder they lengthened legs with attached pig bristles to make stilts, or shortened legs to make stumps, and tested food-carrying ants in a separate channel.

Because the modification was made after the outbound distance had been acquired, outbound and inbound strides differed in length. If stride length underlies the odometer, the ant should misjudge the distance home in a direction set by the change in leg length.
notes: Distance estimation can be tested by changing the length of a stride.
Definition.
An odometer estimates distance traveled.
A stride is one complete movement cycle of a leg.
Training.
Cataglyphis fortis walked to a feeder 10 meters from the nest.
Manipulation.
Pig bristles attached to the legs produced stilts.
Shortened legs produced stumps.
Timing.
The change was made at the feeder, after the outbound distance had been acquired.
Outbound strides and inbound strides therefore differed.
Test.
Food-carrying ants were released into a separate channel and their search was recorded.
Prediction.
If stride length underlies the odometer, the direction of the error follows the change in leg length.
Why stilts and stumps.
Longer legs cover more ground per stride and shorter legs cover less.
The two manipulations push the prediction in opposite directions.
Agreement in both directions makes the test stronger.
Pig bristles.
Attached bristles lengthened the legs into stilts.
Cutting the legs produced stumps.
Summary.
Changing stride length after acquisition tests the odometer directly.

inserts.title: Turning points mark the expected nest distance
paragraphs: Turning points are the places where a searching ant reverses direction in a U-turn. After directed walking toward the expected nest position, the ant begins repeated turns, and the median of the first six turning points marks the centre of its search.

After a normal 10 m outbound journey, ants with lengthened legs searched at 15.30 m, ants with shortened legs at 5.75 m, and normal-legged controls at 10.20 m. The search centre moved in the direction of the change in stride length.

The switch from directed walking to repeated U-turns is a behavioral readout of the distance the ant expects to have covered. A search centred beyond or short of the true nest indicates that the stored estimate was read out with strides of a different length.
notes: The first turns of a search report the distance the ant expects.
Definition.
Turning points are U-turn positions during the search.
The median of the first six identifies the search centre.
Behavior.
Ants walk in a directed way and then switch to repeated U-turns.
Stilts.
Ants with lengthened legs searched at 15.30 meters.
Stumps and controls.
Ants with shortened legs searched at 5.75 meters.
Normal-legged controls searched at 10.20 meters.
Direction of error.
Longer strides produced overshoot and shorter strides produced undershoot.
Meaning.
The search centre reads out the stored distance in the units of the strides used.
Why median of six.
A single turn can be noisy.
The median of the first six turning points gives a stable estimate of the centre of the search.
Controls searched near the true 10 meter distance.
Comparison.
Normal-legged ants searched at 10.20 meters, close to the true separation.
Stilts and stumps departed from it in opposite directions.
Summary.
Search position reports the stored distance.

inserts.title: A tripod gait alternates two sets of legs
paragraphs: A tripod gait alternates two sets of three supporting legs. In Cataglyphis one set combines the left front and hind legs with the right middle leg, and the complementary set uses the remaining three legs. At each step one set supports the body while the other swings.

Wittlinger and colleagues filmed ants with high-speed video at 250 frames per second before and after manipulation. A normal example had a stride length of 13.3 mm at 0.28 m/s, and a stumps-II example kept tripod coordination with a 10.5 mm stride at 0.27 m/s.

The stump ant walked at nearly the same speed with a shorter stride and the same alternating pattern. Shortening the legs reduces how far each step advances the body and leaves the basic coordination of the walking cycle in place.
notes: Gait coordination shows what shortened legs change and what they keep.
Definition.
A tripod gait alternates two sets of three supporting legs.
One set is the left front, left hind and right middle legs.
The other set.
The complementary set uses the remaining three legs.
Recording.
High-speed video at 250 frames per second was taken before and after manipulation.
Normal example.
Stride length was 13.3 millimeters at 0.28 meters per second.
Stumps example.
A stumps-II ant had a 10.5 millimeter stride at 0.27 meters per second.
It retained tripod coordination.
Meaning.
Shortening changes how far each step advances the ant and leaves the coordination pattern in place.
Why coordination matters.
A different gait after shortening would make stride comparisons between groups unclear.
Preserved tripod coordination keeps the comparison to stride length.
The ants carried food during the tests.
Complementary sets.
While one set of three legs is on the ground the other set is in the air.
The alternation repeats every cycle.
Summary.
Shortened legs keep the coordination pattern and reduce the spatial extent of the cycle.

inserts.title: Full width at half maximum measures search spread
paragraphs: The **full width at half maximum** is the width of a distribution measured at half of its peak height. For a search density distribution it describes how broadly an ant spreads its search around the expected nest location, while the center of the distribution estimates that location.
The test channel was divided into 10 cm bins. In the first test the full width at half maximum was 8.3 m for stilts, 6.0 m for normal legs, 5.2 m for stumps I and 4.1 m for stumps II.

Stilts produced the broadest search and stumps II the narrowest. Spread and center both vary with leg length, so the plotted search curves differ in how widely the animal samples positions as well as in where it expects the nest.
notes: A distribution has a centre and a width, and each carries information.
Definition.
Full width at half maximum is the width of a curve at half its peak height.
Search density.
The distribution records how often the ant visits positions.
Its centre estimates the expected nest location.
Binning.
The test channel was divided into 10 centimeter bins.
Widths.
Stilts measured 8.3 meters and normal legs 6.0 meters.
Stumps I measured 5.2 meters and stumps II 4.1 meters.
Ordering.
Stilts gave the broadest search and stumps II the narrowest.
Meaning.
Both the centre and the spread of the search vary with leg length.
Why spread is informative.
Centre and width are separate descriptions of the same curve.
The centre gives the expected nest location.
The width describes how broadly the search is distributed around it.
Interpretation of the numbers.
The widths ranged from 4.1 to 8.3 meters across the four groups.
Longer legs gave broader searches.
Summary.
The distribution carries both a location and a spread.

inserts.title: Stride frequency and stride length are separate
paragraphs: Stride frequency is the number of complete leg cycles per second, measured in hertz, and stride length is the distance advanced during one cycle. Walking speed depends on both, so an ant can run faster by cycling more quickly, by taking longer strides, or by both.

At comparable frequencies, stilt ants had longer relative strides and stump ants shorter relative strides than controls. The investigators used the measured frequency–length relationships to compare animals at 20 Hz.

Comparing animals at one cycle frequency reduces the effect of unequal movement speeds on predicted homing distances. The remaining ordering of stilts, controls and stumps reflects the imposed limb geometry and the distance each stride advances the ant.
notes: Two variables of the walking cycle can both change speed.
Frequency.
Stride frequency is the number of leg cycles per second, in hertz.
Length.
Stride length is the distance advanced during one cycle.
Speed.
Faster walking can come from faster cycles, longer strides, or both.
Observation.
At comparable frequencies stilt ants had longer relative strides.
Stump ants had shorter relative strides than controls.
Standardizing.
Animals were compared at 20 hertz using the measured frequency and length relationships.
Meaning.
The ordering of the leg conditions follows the stride length each limb geometry produces.
Why 20 hertz.
A common frequency puts all animals at a comparable cycle rate.
Differences in stride length then predict differences in homing distance.
The relationships were measured from high-speed records.
Relative stride.
Stride lengths were expressed relative to body size.
This allows animals of different size to be compared.
Summary.
Leg geometry sets the distance advanced per cycle.

inserts.title: Proprioception reports limb position and movement
paragraphs: Proprioception is the sensing of the position and movement of one's own body parts. In an insect leg it supplies information about limb position and movement during each step, and it is one candidate input to a stride integrator.

The 2007 experiments combined a 10 m navigational task with 250-frame-per-second video and leg-length manipulations. Tripod coordination was preserved after shortening, and stride changes were graded with the extent of shortening.

Another candidate input is activity associated with generating the walking rhythm. A stride integrator accumulates information tied to rhythmic locomotion and does not need to register each footfall as a discrete counted object, so graded stride changes yield graded errors in distance.
notes: A stride integrator can draw on several kinds of movement signal.
Definition.
Proprioception is sensing of the position and movement of the body's own parts.
In the leg.
It supplies information about limb position and movement during each step.
Other inputs.
Activity associated with generating the walking rhythm is another candidate.
Integrator.
A stride integrator accumulates information associated with rhythmic locomotion.
It need not count each footfall.
Experiments.
A 10 meter task was combined with 250-frame-per-second video and leg-length manipulations.
Meaning.
Graded stride changes yield graded errors, as an accumulator of movement-linked information predicts.
Why not elapsed time.
A rule based only on elapsed time would give the same distance for different stride lengths.
The graded errors followed stride length.
The tripod pattern was preserved after shortening.
Candidate inputs.
Proprioception reports limb position and movement.
Activity that generates the walking rhythm is another candidate.
Summary.
A stride integrator sums movement-linked information over the journey.

inserts.title: Central complex and mushroom bodies in the ant brain
paragraphs: The central complex is a set of midline brain neuropils implicated in heading and navigation, and the mushroom bodies are paired structures implicated in memory-based processing. A neuropil is a region containing neuronal processes and synapses.

Grob and colleagues labelled Cataglyphis brains with anti-synapsin antibodies and fluorescent phalloidin, which marks actin-rich structures. The preparations identified mushroom-body collar microglomeruli and giant synapses in the lateral complex, with a 200 µm scale bar for the whole brain and 10 µm bars for the insets.

The two visual pathways reach different integration centres, so the structures can be measured separately after the same experience. Counts of synaptic structures give each pathway its own anatomical endpoint.
notes: Navigation involves distinct neuropils, each measured on its own.
Neuropil.
A neuropil is a region of neuronal processes and synapses.
Central complex.
It lies at the midline and is implicated in heading and navigation.
Mushroom bodies.
These paired structures are implicated in memory-based processing.
Labels.
Anti-synapsin antibodies and fluorescent phalloidin were used.
Phalloidin marks actin-rich structures.
Structures counted.
Mushroom-body collar microglomeruli and giant synapses in the lateral complex were identified.
Scale bars were 200 micrometers for the whole brain and 10 micrometers for insets.
Meaning.
Each visual pathway gives a separate anatomical endpoint after the same experience.
Why scale bars matter.
The whole-brain image gives overall position.
The insets show individual synaptic structures at higher magnification.
Both pathways can then be quantified in the same animals.
Lateral complex.
Giant synapses in the lateral complex lie along the sky-compass pathway.
They are counted in the same preparations.
Summary.
Separate structures give separate measures of experience.

inserts.title: Structural plasticity is a change in anatomy
paragraphs: Structural plasticity is an experience-associated change in neuronal anatomy, such as neuropil volume or synaptic organization. It differs from an acute firing-rate response to a sensory stimulus, which changes within seconds and leaves anatomy unchanged.

After three days, natural learning walks increased the size-corrected central-complex volume of _Cataglyphis nodus_ relative to dark controls. Passive light exposure and learning walks under a stationary polarization filter did not produce the same increase.

Correcting volume for body size ensures that larger ants do not appear to have larger brain regions through body size alone. The central complex grows with active experience of changing celestial information and not with light exposure alone. Larger bodies carry larger brains, so the correction keeps the comparison between treatments.
notes: Experience can change the structure of the brain, and not only its activity.
Definition.
Structural plasticity is an experience-associated change in anatomy.
Examples are neuropil volume and synaptic organization.
Contrast.
An acute firing-rate response to a stimulus is a different kind of change.
Experiment.
Novices performed learning walks for three days.
Result.
Natural learning walks increased central-complex volume relative to dark controls.
Passive light and a stationary filter did not.
Size correction.
Brain volumes were corrected for body size.
Raw tissue amounts alone would be misleading.
Meaning.
Active experience with changing celestial information drives central-complex growth.
Why correct for body size.
Larger Cataglyphis workers have larger bodies.
Without correction a body-size difference could look like an effect of experience.
Size-corrected volumes make dark controls and learning-walk groups comparable.
Comparison groups.
Dark controls, passive light exposure and a stationary filter were compared with natural learning walks.
Only natural learning walks raised central-complex volume.
Summary.
Anatomy changes with experience of a changing sky.

inserts.title: Helmholtz coils set the magnetic field
paragraphs: A Helmholtz coil system generates a controlled magnetic field in an experimental volume. Currents in the coils can add to or cancel the geomagnetic field, which is Earth's magnetic field and provides a directional reference independent of the sun's daily movement.

Grob and colleagues installed a three-dimensional coil system around a 60 × 60 cm platform connected to a _Cataglyphis nodus_ nest. Novices performed learning walks over three consecutive days, and the natural total field at the site was about 46.1 µT with a horizontal component of 26.6 µT.

The coils change magnetic information while the natural panorama and celestial environment remain available. Several magnetic conditions can be compared with dark interior-worker controls to assess experience-associated brain changes caused by the magnetic reference.
notes: Coils make the magnetic field an experimental variable.
Definition.
A Helmholtz coil system generates controlled magnetic fields in a volume.
Geomagnetic field.
Earth's field gives a directional reference independent of the sun's movement.
Set-up.
A three-dimensional coil system surrounded a 60 by 60 centimeter platform.
The platform was connected to a Cataglyphis nodus nest.
Field values.
The natural total field was about 46.1 microtesla.
Its horizontal component was 26.6 microtesla.
Experience.
Novices performed learning walks over three consecutive days.
Controls.
Dark interior-worker controls provide the comparison for brain changes.
Why coils and not a magnet.
Coils produce a uniform field that can be set in each of three directions.
The field can also be cancelled almost completely.
These options make several magnetic conditions possible.
Field components.
The horizontal and vertical components of the field can be handled separately.
The natural total field was about 46.1 microtesla.
Summary.
Coils turn the magnetic field into a variable that the experimenter controls.

inserts.title: A pirouette is a rotation during a learning walk
paragraphs: A pirouette is a rotation around the ant's body axis during a learning walk. Under natural conditions the longest pauses in these rotations are directed toward the nest, which gives a measurable orientation behavior near the nest entrance.

In the horizontal-elimination condition the coils cancelled the horizontal field component and retained a downward vertical field of about 37.5 µT. The longest stopping directions no longer clustered toward the nest in the published angular distributions, which used 10° bins.

The direction of the longest pause serves as the measure of where the ant looks. Loss of nest-directed pauses when only the horizontal component is removed indicates that horizontal magnetic information contributes to the novices' nest-directed behavior.
notes: Learning walks include rotations whose pauses can be scored.
Definition.
A pirouette is a rotation around the ant's body axis during a learning walk.
Natural pattern.
The longest pauses are directed toward the nest.
This is a measurable orientation near the entrance.
Manipulation.
The coils cancelled the horizontal field component.
A downward vertical field of about 37.5 microtesla remained.
Analysis.
Directions of the longest stops were plotted in 10 degree bins.
Result.
The longest stops no longer clustered toward the nest.
Meaning.
Horizontal magnetic information contributes to nest-directed behavior in this condition.
Why the longest pause.
The longest stop during a pirouette marks the direction of gaze.
Under natural conditions this direction points toward the nest.
Losing that pattern is a clear behavioral readout.
Field conditions.
The vertical field of 37.5 microtesla remained when the horizontal field was cancelled.
Complete elimination is a different condition.
Summary.
Pauses toward the nest report the use of horizontal magnetic information.

inserts.title: A goal vector stores a destination
paragraphs: A **goal vector** stores the direction and distance to a destination relative to the nest. Each feeder therefore has its own vector, and the ant can use either one at any time during a search.

Voegeli and colleagues trained Cataglyphis ants to feeders A and B at nest distances of 4.5 m and 5.7 m. A test channel connected the feeder positions across a 4.1 m separation, and only one nest-channel entrance was open at a time.

The arrangement separates experience with each nest-to-feeder route from experience with the connecting route. Ants were never trained to follow the proposed shortcut, so a search toward the second feeder must come from the stored goal vectors combined with the ongoing path integrator.
notes: A stored destination can be tested without training the shortcut.
Definition.
A goal vector is a remembered direction and distance to a destination, relative to the nest.
Shortcut.
A shortcut joins familiar destinations along a route not used in training.
Training.
Ants learned feeders A and B in separate channels.
Nest distances were 4.5 meters and 5.7 meters.
Test channel.
It connected the feeder positions across a 4.1 meter separation.
Only one nest-channel entrance was open at a time.
Design.
Experience with each nest-to-feeder route was separated from experience with the connecting route.
Meaning.
Searching toward the second feeder reflects stored goal vectors and the ongoing path integrator.
Why hidden feeders.
Feeders were hidden below the channel floor.
An approaching ant could not steer toward a visible food cup.
Searching therefore depends on stored information.
Goal vector and shortcut.
A goal vector is a stored destination.
A shortcut is a new route between known destinations.
Summary.
Training the two feeders separately tests stored goals without teaching the shortcut.

2: **Path integration** is the continual updating of direction and distance from a starting point using information gathered during movement. The **home vector** specifies the direction and distance back to the nest, so it summarizes the whole outward trip in one vector rather than retracing each turn. It is a computation that runs continuously, so the ant always holds an estimate of where the nest lies.

Müller and Wehner recorded a natural foraging trip of Cataglyphis fortis in Tunisia. The outward path measured 354.5 m, while the maximum distance from the nest was 113.2 m. After finding food, the ant returned along a comparatively direct inbound route, so the homing path was far shorter than the outward path.

The difference between outward path length and nest displacement separates route retracing from **vector-guided homing**. A direct return after a winding 354.5 m outward path reflects a vector that sums every segment of the trip into one direction and one distance. The vector is recalculated from the full path, so the inbound route can be short even when the outbound route was long.
3: Passive displacement changes an ant's geographical position without supplying the walking movements that normally update its **home vector**. A displaced ant therefore expresses a direction that matches its earlier position rather than the nest's actual location. The ant's internal estimate therefore stays fixed at the place where the displacement occurred.

Müller and Wehner captured a food-carrying ant at its feeding location and released it elsewhere in open terrain. The subsequent course was compared with the geographical nest direction and with the course predicted from its recorded outbound trajectory, on a 10 m spatial scale. The released ant was free to walk, so its first heading reveals the vector it held at release.

The course retained information from the outward journey despite the transfer. The test separates movement-derived navigation from immediate attraction to the true nest, because the course after release points to where the nest would lie had the ant not been moved. The ant's direction after release is therefore a measure of its stored vector.
5: **Systematic error** means a directional deviation that varies predictably with an experimental manipulation, and it differs from random scatter among journeys. Müller and Wehner measured the angular difference between the true homeward direction and the course expressed after two-leg training. Each outbound turn adds a small error to the estimate, and the errors accumulate along the path.

With outbound legs of 10 m and 5 m, the error increased as the turning angle approached about 150°, reaching about 20° in the published measurements. The error returned toward zero at the straight and reversed arrangements, so its size depends on the geometry of the outbound turn. The error grows with the angle up to that point.

The angle-dependent pattern supports an approximate **updating rule** under these conditions. Because the error is systematic rather than random, the integrator follows a consistent rule that can be described mathematically. The rule therefore predicts the error for any tested turning angle. The prediction holds for every turning angle that the experiment tested, so the rule describes the full set of measurements.
8: Route geometry determines how an approximate path integrator accumulates error. A sharp sustained turn produces a large deviation, whereas turns in opposite directions partly cancel their effects on the estimated homeward direction. The sign of each turn determines whether successive errors add or cancel. The effect of each turn therefore depends on the turn that came before it.

Müller and Wehner compared the proposed updating rule with recorded natural foraging paths. In the displaced example the expressed course departed from the real nest direction by about 20°, in agreement with the direction predicted from that ant's outward trajectory. Both paths were recorded in the field, so the prediction is tested in natural conditions.

Natural Cataglyphis paths rarely contain the repeated sharp backward turns that generate the largest experimental errors. For the turning patterns an ant meets on a real foraging trip, the approximation keeps homing errors small, and landmarks and searching cover the cases where the vector alone is insufficient. The natural route therefore keeps the error small, consistent with a navigation system adapted to ordinary foraging routes.
12: Wittlinger and colleagues extended the odometer experiment with two degrees of leg shortening. **Tarsomeres** are the distal segments of an insect leg, and the **tibia** lies proximal to the tarsus. Removing these regions changes the effective length of the walking limb. Each degree of shortening changes the stride length, which is the quantity the experiment varies.

Stumps I lacked the distal tarsal segments, whereas stumps II had the distal half of the tibia removed. A third group carried bristle stilts, and normal-legged ants provided the comparison. All groups had acquired the same 10 m outbound feeder distance before the first test. Each group is defined by its anatomical change, so the groups can be compared directly.

The graded manipulation allows comparison of different reductions in stride length rather than treating all shortened legs as one condition. All groups shared the same navigational task, so differences in homing distance can be attributed to the degree of leg shortening. The comparison therefore isolates the effect of leg length on the search.
14: A shorter stride covers less ground during each locomotor cycle. If outbound distance is stored in relation to movement cycles, shortening the legs after that journey makes the inbound estimate end before the original feeder-to-nest distance. The estimate of distance is built from the number of cycles, so each step of the stride matters.

In the expanded experiment, normal-legged ants searched at 10.20 m, stumps-I ants at 6.95 m and stumps-II ants at 5.75 m. Stilts produced searches at 15.30 m. These values were measured after a 10 m outbound run through the training channel. These measured distances all come from the same outbound run, so they can be compared directly.

The graded undershoot is consistent with a stride integrator rather than a fixed physical-distance readout independent of locomotion. Stumps II removed more of the leg than stumps I and produced the shorter search, so greater shortening produced greater undershoot. The graded pattern shows that the search distance scales with the stride, as the integrator predicts.
15: A **search density distribution** records how often an ant visits positions during its search. Its center estimates the expected nest location, while its width describes how broadly the animal distributes its search around that estimate. The distribution is the record of where the ant searched, so its shape carries the search information.

The test channel was divided into 10 cm bins. In the first test the full width at half maximum was 8.3 m for stilts, 6.0 m for normal legs, 5.2 m for stumps I and 4.1 m for stumps II. The search curves therefore differed in spread as well as in center.

Longer strides spread the search over more distance and shorter strides over less, so the width of the distribution scales with stride length as the center does. Center and width are two behavioral readouts of the same stride-based process. Stride length therefore sets both the place where the search is centered and the spread around it.
21: A **stride integrator** accumulates information associated with rhythmic locomotion. It accumulates movement-linked signals rather than counting discrete footfalls. Possible inputs include proprioception, sensory information about limb position and movement, and activity associated with generating the walking rhythm. Each input is a signal that changes with every stride. The integrator therefore keeps a running total that grows with each stride the ant takes.

The 2007 experiments combined a 10 m navigational task with 250-frame-per-second video and leg-length manipulations. The preserved tripod pattern and the graded stride changes were both consistent with accumulation of movement-linked information rather than a fixed elapsed-time rule. The graded pattern therefore matches a process that accumulates stride-linked information. Each leg-length treatment changes the size of the stride, which changes the total that the integrator accumulates.

Proprioceptive signals, limb-position feedback and the motor commands that generate the walking rhythm are the candidate inputs to the integrator. Each carries information proportional to stride, which is why a stride integrator can account for graded distance errors. Together these inputs supply the stride-based estimate that the experiments measured. Each of these signals scales with the distance covered, which links the stride to the integrated estimate.
34: A magnetic cue does not have to point toward natural magnetic north to serve as a usable short-term directional reference. What matters is whether its direction remains stable during each individual learning walk. The ant needs only a direction that stays stable during the walk to use the cue. The cue functions because it stays stable during each walk, even though its alignment changes over the day.

In the magnetic-plus-solar condition, the horizontal vector was adjusted every 10 seconds to follow the sun's azimuth over the day. Individual walks lasted seconds to minutes, and the ants retained nest-directed longest stops despite the vector's changing geographical alignment. The solar azimuth moved steadily during the day, and the vector followed it at each 10-second update.

A magnetic vector that follows the solar azimuth still serves as a usable reference within each short learning walk, so nest-directed look-backs persist. The manipulation makes magnetic and celestial directions covary over the day, which removes their natural changing angular relationship. The ants therefore keep orienting toward the nest throughout each walk.
38: A **goal vector** specifies a remembered direction and distance to a destination relative to the nest. A shortcut connects familiar destinations along a route that was never used during training, and such behavior can be produced by stored vectors without requiring a metric cognitive map. Each goal vector is tied to a feeder, so the ant can select the vector that matches its goal.

Voegeli and colleagues trained Cataglyphis ants to feeders A and B in separate channels, at nest distances of 4.5 m and 5.7 m. The test channel connected the two feeder positions across a 4.1 m separation, and only one nest-channel entrance was open at a time. The two feeders were therefore separated by a fixed distance, which the test channel spanned.

The channel arrangement separates experience with each nest-to-feeder route from experience with the connecting route. The ants were never trained to follow the proposed shortcut, so a search toward the second feeder must come from stored goal vectors and the ongoing path integrator. The test thus isolates the effect of stored goal vectors from any learned route.
40: A **one-feeder control** establishes the search pattern expected without memory of a second food source. This comparison distinguishes a general tendency to widen a search from a directional bias toward another learned destination. The control establishes what a search looks like before any second destination is learned. The control makes the baseline explicit.

Control ants visited only feeder A before testing. After food removal their searches concentrated around the former feeder position and spread approximately symmetrically on its two sides. Distance from the starting point was measured in meters along the connecting test channel. The searches after food removal reflect the position of the single feeder the ants had learned.

The symmetric baseline sets the reference for interpreting the two-feeder experiments. A later directional shift is attributed to the second feeder, because ants with one feeder search equally on both sides of the channel. The symmetric pattern therefore indicates a neutral search, against which any directional bias in the two-feeder tests can be measured.
45: A **metric cognitive map** represents spatial relationships among familiar places in a common coordinate system. Novel shortcutting is often taken as evidence for such a map, yet the same behavior can follow from simpler stored vectors combined with continuous updating of self-motion. A map of this kind predicts that the ant can take any route between learned places, not only the routes it has traveled.

Cataglyphis ants trained separately to feeders 4.5 m and 5.7 m from the nest searched along their previously untraveled connecting route. The controlled A-to-B test showed flexible navigation toward a second goal without prior experience of that particular route. The distances of the two feeders from the nest were fixed by the training, and the test used the same feeders.

Shortcutting is therefore a diagnostic that depends on the model of navigation considered. The observed behavior is compatible with a nest-referenced vector system, which accounts for the shortcut without the stronger assumption of a metric cognitive map. The interpretation therefore depends on which model the shortcut is evaluated against, and the vector model explains the observed route.
